name: Garage Dreams
description: How a hobbyist kit became a machine on every desk: the chips, the companies, the programs and the people behind the personal computer revolution.

checkpoints.name: Kits and garages
checkpoints.note: Hobbyists build computers from kits such as the Altair, and two young friends in California start Apple. The Apple II, TRS-80 and PET of 1977 are among the first mass-market machines sold ready to use, and VisiCalc gives businesses a reason to buy.

checkpoints.name: The beige box
checkpoints.note: IBM enters with the IBM PC and an open design that lets clones such as Compaq follow. MS-DOS and Lotus 1-2-3 dominate offices, while cheap home machines from Commodore and Sinclair fill children's bedrooms.

checkpoints.name: Mouse and windows
checkpoints.note: The Macintosh, Amiga and Atari ST bring pictures and sound, and Windows slowly turns DOS into a graphical system. Commodore collapses as the PC and the Mac settle in as the two main camps.

checkpoints.name: Everyone online
checkpoints.note: Windows 95 brings the PC to nearly every home and the internet makes it essential. Apple returns with the iMac, and the tiny Raspberry Pi brings the kit-computer spirit back for a new generation.
